name: MIND diet

lead: The MIND diet (Mediterranean-DASH Intervention for Neurodegenerative Delay) was developed by a Rush University Medical Center team led by nutritional epidemiologist Martha Clare Morris and published in 2015. It combines elements of the Mediterranean and DASH diets with foods linked to brain health: leafy greens, berries, nuts, beans, whole grains, fish, poultry and olive oil, with limits on butter, red meat, cheese, pastries and fried food.

It is a brain-health diet rather than a looks protocol. People follow it to eat in a whole-food pattern that supports general health, and a consistent produce-rich diet is also how many people approach skin, weight and energy.

paras: Followers aim for daily whole grains and vegetables, leafy greens most days, berries and nuts through the week, beans several times weekly, poultry and fish, and olive oil as the main cooking fat, while limiting butter, sweets, red meat, cheese and fried or fast food.

No notable risks from the food pattern itself; the recommended daily glass of wine in the original description is a choice, not a requirement. People with medical conditions or allergies tailor it with a clinician. Evidence for protecting cognition is mixed.

angle.text: The MIND diet is a plant-forward whole-food pattern. People who adopt it for brain health also describe it as supporting energy and weight management, which feed into how they look.

lead: The MIND diet, short for Mediterranean-DASH Intervention for Neurodegenerative Delay, is an eating pattern designed by a Rush University Medical Center team including nutritional epidemiologist Martha Clare Morris to slow cognitive decline, published in 2015 [1]. It hybridises the Mediterranean and DASH diets, because neither was developed specifically for brain health [1].

Its appearance angle is general: it is a whole-food pattern rich in vegetables, berries, nuts, beans and fish and low in sweets, fried food and red meat, the sort of pattern people also adopt for skin, energy and body composition. The diet itself was not designed as a cosmetic protocol, and no study has examined it for appearance.

Observational studies associate higher adherence with slower cognitive decline [2][3]. A 2023 randomised trial reported in the New England Journal of Medicine compared it with a mildly restricted control diet [4].
infobox: Martha Clare Morris and colleagues, Rush University Medical Center

paras: Wikipedia lists the recommended elements as at least three servings of whole grains daily, six or more servings of leafy greens weekly, one other vegetable daily, five servings of nuts weekly, three or more servings of beans weekly, two or more servings of berries weekly, poultry twice weekly, fish once weekly and olive oil as the main cooking oil, with wine optional at one glass daily [1]. The discouraged list includes more than a tablespoon of butter or margarine daily, more than five servings of pastries and sweets weekly, more than four servings of red meat weekly, more than one serving of cheese weekly and more than one serving of fried or fast food weekly [1].

The Rush team published two papers in 2015: one reported that higher MIND adherence was associated with slower cognitive decline [2] and another that it was associated with reduced incidence of Alzheimer's disease [3]. Wikipedia notes these were correlational and need replication [1].

A 2022 systematic review of 13 studies found that 78 percent reported a positive association between MIND adherence and global cognition in older adults [5]. A 2023 meta-analysis of cohort studies including a Chinese cohort of 4,066 people found higher MIND scores were associated with better global cognitive function [6]. A 2024 review of 40 articles examined dementia and other brain aging outcomes [7].

A 2019 Australian cohort study found MIND, but not the Mediterranean diet, related to 12-year incidence of cognitive impairment [8]. A systematic review of randomised trials found only one small MIND trial among those it covered [9]. A 2025 randomised trial of overweight diabetic women with insomnia examined sleep, mental health and BDNF [10].

The 2023 New England Journal of Medicine trial tested the MIND diet for prevention of cognitive decline in older persons against a control diet [4]. Follow-up analyses of that trial examined effect modifiers, carotenoid links with APOE genotype and its use as a genetic resource for precision nutrition [11][12][13]. A 2025 trial of oral nutrition supplementation in older adults is a separate intervention [14].

timeline.event: Rush University researchers publish MIND diet findings on cognitive decline and Alzheimer's incidence. [2][3]
